Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine his future, the report added. Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The reports come days after Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, as Nvidia's board investigates whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Nvidia's shares were down about 8% in after-hours trading.

House Republicans push for Nvidia's Huang to testify, float subpoena over spy allegations Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 03:58 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 03:58 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

A trio of House Republicans are unlikely to allow Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to send his company's general counsel to answer questions on his behalf about his alleged relationship with a Chinese spy, according to a person familiar with the discussions. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast and two other top Republican lawmakers on November 4 asked Huang to provide a closed-door briefing about a New York Times report alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Mast is open to issuing a congressional subpoena if Huang doesn’t respond to their request, his spokesperson said. Lawmakers need support from colleagues to issue a subpoena, and the rules to do so vary by committee. The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, with Nvidia at the center because its advanced chips are widely used to train and run cutting-edge models. Washington has spent years trying to restrict China's access to those chips on national security grounds, and the allegations involving Huang have intensified lawmakers' concerns about whether export controls and other safeguards are strong enough to prevent sensitive US technology from benefiting Beijing. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar, part of the group of lawmakers who requested the briefing, said on Fox Business that Huang had until 5 p.m. ET (2200 GMT) Wednesday to decide whether he would agree to meet with lawmakers behind closed doors. “If he doesn't agree to that or submit an additional date, I believe there will likely be subpoenas for him to appear,” he said. A spokesperson for Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (Reporting Alexandra Alper and Courtney Rozen in Washington, Karen Freifeld in New York; Editing by Sonali Paul)

item.content:encoded:
Russia, Ukraine reach deal on prisoner swap as US says lack of trust holds back talks Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 03:58 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 03:58 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators agreed to a major prisoner exchange at two days of peace talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Wednesday, but US mediators said differences remained on major issues, including territory. At their first negotiations in nine months, the two countries agreed in principle to exchange prisoners of war and to determine the numbers on Thursday. US envoy Jared Kushner said the new swap would be the "biggest humanitarian release of prisoners" in the 4-1/2-year-old war, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said its scope would be "significant." Both Russia and Ukraine said that progress had been made in the Abu Dhabi talks and negotiations would continue. But there was little else in the way of concrete breakthroughs announced after the US-brokered meetings. Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said mediators were appealing to each side's interests to end Europe's biggest conflict since World War Two and he expressed confidence they would find a pathway to peace. Despite public optimism from Trump, there has been no sign of major compromises on the main issues after more than 4-1/2 years of war since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Kyiv has strongly rejected Russian President Vladimir Putin's demands to surrender the whole of the eastern region of Donbas in return for peace. With talks deadlocked on land, US mediators have tried to steer discussions towards postwar security guarantees and reconstruction. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this," Kushner said, adding that the talks had touched on territorial issues and that these would be the hardest to resolve. "I think this was a good first step," he said. Kushner said he and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday for talks with Putin, where they will raise the question of adding European partners to the talks, who Kushner said must be at the table. The US negotiators then plan to fly to Ireland to meet with Zelenskiy, who is due to attend a meeting of European leaders there. Zelenskiy told reporters in Dublin on Wednesday that Ukraine was focused on achieving progress on an accord this year. "A lot will depend today on the format of the dialogue of the American and Russian sides tomorrow... I believe it is also very important for the Americans...to achieve a result this year, in my view, given what we are seeing happening," he said. "And it seems to me that they really do want this very much." ATTACKS CONTINUE Russia and Ukraine accused each other of launching attacks overnight, despite the Abu Dhabi peace talks. Russia hit sixelectricity substations in central Ukraine, Ukrainian officials said, and an attack on a market in the Odesa region killed three people. A Ukrainian drone attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region, local officials said. Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said the talks had been tough, with Russia's delegation arriving with "strict directives", but the conversations provided "good momentum" towards reaching a solution by the end of the year. Although European officials and NATO representatives met US and Ukrainian envoys in Abu Dhabi, Russia's delegation refused to meet them. Arakhamia said future peace talks must be multilateral and include Europe at the table. Russia's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian state TV he thought a peace deal was closer after the talks but "a great deal depends on Ukraine, on the US stance, and on whether Europe comes to its senses". Russia has repeatedly criticised European military support for Ukraine. As the Trump administration has scaled back its direct aid to Ukraine, Europe has become the leading provider of finance and military support to Kyiv. Reaffirming Moscow's long-standing demands, Medinsky told Russian state news agency TASS that "every inch" of Russian land would be returned to Russia — an apparent reference to Putin's insistence that Ukraine surrender all of the Donbas. Ukraine had hoped the Abu Dhabi talks would make progress towards a ceasefire on Black Sea grain shipments as a means of de-escalation, but Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, on a visit to Turkey, said Kyiv was still awaiting a Russian response. FRONT LINE STATIC Russian forces control about a fifth of Ukraine, much of it captured before the 2022 invasion, and their progress on the battlefield has slowed this year. With the front line largely static, Moscow has been pounding Ukrainian cities and energy sites, while Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure. Russian officials are calling for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before tackling the specifics of the war. Before its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russia demanded the withdrawal of NATO forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997, which the alliance rejected. European officials say wider security talks should only come after a ceasefire, and that Russia should not be allowed to influence Europe's security arrangements or be rewarded for starting the war. Trump said last week the war was close to being settled in a "big beautiful agreement" that could include security guarantees for Europe. He has frequently predicted breakthroughs that have not materialised.

US Treasury chief Bessent moved to military base after Iranian threats, sources say Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 03:57 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 03:57 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has recently moved from his Washington, DC, residence to a US military base after Iranian threats against his life, two people familiar with the matter said on Tuesday. The New York Times first reported the move. The Times said the severity of the threats was not immediately clear. A senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters late last month that Iranian plots against US personnel and American citizens had reached an advanced stage. Bessent has led the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The crucial waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. The economic pressure campaign, which coincides with a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, has included sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and other financial services firms facilitating transactions with Iran. "The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a US Treasury spokesperson said in an emailed statement. A person familiar with the matter said security concerns surrounding Bessent began to increase after the Wall Street Journal reported in January 2025 that he had bought a Georgetown mansion for $12.5 million. The Journal story included an aerial photo of the property, which the person said allowed it to be geolocated. The person declined to address the timing of the government's decision to move Bessent. Contacted on Wednesday, a day after Reuters initially published its story, the Journal did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the security issue. Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil. The New York Times reported that US officials have noted that Iran's ability to carry out large-scale attacks in the US and other territories overseas is limited. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon during the war have killed thousands and displaced millions. American and Israeli attacks have also killed top Iranian officials, including late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
